q: What is the underlying mechanism of myasthenia gravis?
o: Antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Antibodies to post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
why: IgG against the nicotinic AChR activates complement, reducing receptor numbers and post-synaptic folds. Antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels cause Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

q: How do patients with myasthenia gravis respond to neuromuscular blocking drugs?
o: Sensitive to suxamethonium, resistant to non-depolarisers
Relatively resistant to suxamethonium, very sensitive to non-depolarisers
why: Fewer functioning receptors mean resistance to suxamethonium (higher dose, possibly prolonged) and marked sensitivity to non-depolarisers: use reduced doses titrated against train-of-four.

q: After thymectomy, a patient on high-dose pyridostigmine develops weakness with salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Excess ACh from over-treatment causes a cholinergic crisis with a SLUDGE picture. Atropine treats the muscarinic features but not the nicotinic weakness.

q: Which is a risk factor for needing post-operative ventilation after thymectomy?
o: Bulbar symptoms and reduced vital capacity
why: Risk factors include disease over 6 years, bulbar or respiratory symptoms, vital capacity under 2–2.9 L, previous myasthenic crisis, pyridostigmine over 750 mg/day, chronic lung disease, blood loss over 1 L and high antibody titres.

q: In what proportion of patients with myasthenia gravis is the thymus abnormal?
why: The thymus is abnormal in around 75% (mostly hyperplasia, with thymoma in around 15%).

q: How can intubating conditions be achieved for thymectomy while avoiding neuromuscular blockers?
o: Propofol induction then deepening with a volatile agent
why: Propofol induction and deepening with a volatile often gives adequate conditions. If a non-depolariser is needed, use small titrated doses with quantitative monitoring and have sugammadex available.

q: A patient with suspected Guillain–Barré syndrome has a lumbar puncture. What is the typical finding?
o: Raised white cell count with normal protein
why: CSF protein is raised. Nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating or axonal pattern; MRI can show anterior nerve root enhancement.

q: Which feature most strongly indicates that a patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome needs ventilatory support?
o: Bulbar weakness with inability to cough or protect the airway
why: Indications include bulbar involvement, autonomic instability, rising CO2 and rising fatigue with a falling FVC. EGRIS estimates the risk of needing ventilation.

q: Which antibody is associated with the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome?
why: Anti-GQ1b is associated with Miller Fisher syndrome (ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia); anti-GM1 with classic GBS.

q: Why should suxamethonium be avoided in a patient with motor neurone disease?
o: Risk of hyperkalaemia from extrajunctional receptors
why: Denervation causes extrajunctional nicotinic receptors (fetal gamma subunit) that stay open longer, so suxamethonium can cause severe hyperkalaemia. Patients are also sensitive to non-depolarisers.
